title: Black Caucus lays out legislative priorities for 2026 session, notches a win
summary: The Legislative Black Caucus of Maryland notched a victory on its expanded list of legislative priorities Thursday, when the House and Senate approved a 287(g) ban the same day caucus members unveiled their agenda.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 12, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 12, 2026

The Legislative Black Caucus of Maryland notched a victory on its expanded list of legislative priorities Thursday, the same day caucus members unveiled their agenda.

The Senate voted 32-13 and the House voted 99-38 vote to approve emergency legislation that would prohibit agreements between local law enforcement agencies and federal immigration authorities. The bills now go to Gov. Wes Moore (D), who has indicated he will sign the bills, but his office did not respond to a request on when that might be.

Del. Frank Conaway Jr. (D-Baltimore City) was the only Democrat to vote against the measure that would end agreements between Immigration and Customs Enforcement and nine Maryland counties: Allegany, Carroll, Cecil, Frederick, Harford, Garrett, St. Mary’s, Washington and Wicomico.

Senate Bill 245 and House Bill 444 were sponsored by two members of the Black Caucus, Sen. William C. Smith Jr. (D-Montgomery) and Del. Nicole Williams (D-Prince George’s), and were the first wins for the caucus, coming less than a month into the three-month legislative session.

“This big piece of legislation done so early sends a strong message to every Marylander that the state of Maryland is going to stand up and protect everyone in our community, and particularly immigrants,” Smith said after the Senate vote. “We’re going to stand up against the lawless actions of ICE, the unconstitutional actions of ICE and this [federal] administration. It’s a tremendous day.”

The 287(g) prohibition was just one of a wide range of bills identified as priorities Thursday by the Black Caucus, on topics including civil rights, economic empowerment, education, health and housing.

One new measure on the list is House Bill 552, sponsored by Del. Jeffrie Long Jr. (D-Calvert and Prince George’s). It  calls for an independent investigation of property near the Cheltenham Veterans Cemetery in Prince George’s County that may hold unmarked graves of youth from the former House of Reformation and Instruction for Colored Children.

The bill calls for a deep dive on “the history, operations, and resident deaths” at the facility and the wooded area that was its cemetery. That site, with about 300 gravestones and cinder blocks that mark where some of the Black boys were buried from the 19th into the 20th centuries. The overgrown wooded area abuts the well-manicured veterans cemetery.

The investigation would include determining the number of individuals buried at the site, collecting DNA samples and connecting them with any living family members and reviewing available records from state archives, the Department of Juvenile Services, state Department of Health and other state or local agencies “to identify every child who died at the House of Reformation and Instruction for Colored Children.”

A bill hearing is scheduled Feb. 19 before the Government, Labor and Elections Committee.

One returning measure the caucus hopes get to the governor’s desk is a bill that would end the practice of automatically charging youth as adults for some offenses. Lawmakers and advocates have been pursuing that change for several years.

The Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee, which Smith chairs, held a hearing on Senate Bill 323 last week that seeks to raise the age at which a juvenile would be tried as an adult for certain crimes, from 14 to 16. The bill, sponsored by Smith among others, would take several of the 33 offenses that now land a youth in adult court, and send those cases straight to juvenile court instead, for charges such as second-degree rape, third-degree sex offense and certain firearms offenses.

One change from last year’s legislation is that a youth previously convicted of a felony and then charged as an adult, would have their case automatically tried in adult court, Smith said.

The House version was reviewed Thursday by the Judiciary Committee. It is sponsored by committee chair and caucus member Del. J. Sandy Bartlett (D-Anne Arundel), who was joined at the witness table by four heavyweight supporters: Betsy Fox Tolentino, acting secretary for Juvenile Services; Maryland Public Defender Natasha Dartigue; Attorney General Anthony Brown; and Dorothy Lennig, executive director of the Governor’s Office of Crime Prevention and Policy.

“I am big on getting done what I can do when I can, and that’s what’s happening here,” Bartlett said.

Del. Kym Taylor (D-Prince George’s) noted that eight states currently require all juvenile cases go straight to juvenile court and wondered, “Why aren’t we considering that as well?”

Police and prosecutors have routinely opposed the measure, which was the case Thursday: Witnesses against the bill included Baltimore City State’s Attorney Ivan Bates (D), who is also president of the Maryland State’s Attorney’s Association. He said the system is not prepared for the changes proposed in the bill.

“I believe an extremely complex bill that if passed now without addressing the countless levels of systemic deficiencies that currently exist within the juvenile system will lead to an explosion of violent crime committed by juveniles,” Bates said.

“While I sincerely believe … Acting DJS Secretary Besty [Fox] Tolentino and her team are doing all they can to try and remedy these issues, the fact remains that there are far too many issues to be addressed within the current juvenile system,” he said.
